events.description:
Join us for an evening of Stoic philosophy and discussion. We'll kick off the event with a short presentation exploring one of the core ideas of Stoicism, focusing on its real-world application with some practices drawn from the texts. Following the presentation, we'll break into smaller groups for a lightly-facilitated discussion about the topic.

This week, we’ll be discussing how thinking about death in the right way can help us stop wasting our lives. We'll talk about how we waste our time, what we should be spending it on instead, and how to finish our lives each day. We'll also discuss a mindfulness practice designed to help us remember that not even the next hour is guaranteed.

Here's the video we'll be watching: https://youtu.be/G1nM9UCJCIs?si=ES0EKX-x82KWYV&t=11614*x82KWYV*&t=11614

And here's the text, along with the rest of the resources for the course: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-6r2KFyv7f-vChnX-9eKovdFsQ6DYoc_CV5RZtJb9XA/edit?usp=sharing

Thanks so much for your interest, and please remember:

"There is no such thing as good or bad fortune for the individual; we live in common. events.title: Accepting and Coping with the Grim Facts of Life
events.summary: Some of it is just bad. It isn't a lesson, it isn't a test, and nobody is going to arrive and explain what it was for.
events.description:
Some of it is just bad. It isn't a lesson, it isn't a test, and nobody is going to arrive and explain what it was for.

This chapter starts there and never tries to talk you out of it. What it asks instead is a narrower question: given that it's true, how do you want to live alongside it?

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• they know life isn't fair, and still catch themselves protesting that it should be
• the protest changes nothing and is very hard to put down
• "acceptance" sounds like being asked to be fine with it
• the people who seem to have made peace with something look either enlightened or defeated, and neither is appealing
• the energy spent objecting to what happened was needed for what comes next
• the demand that things be otherwise is so constant it doesn't register as a demand

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — spends most of its length on beliefs you can dispute and change. This chapter deals with what's left over. Some things cannot be fixed, reframed, or dissolved by clearer thinking, and the question becomes what you do with what you cannot change. Accepting a fact is not approving of it. You can see something clearly, call it what it is, want it to be otherwise — and stop insisting that reality was supposed to be different.

We'll get into:
• the difference between accepting something and being fine with it
• why the demand persists long after we know it changes nothing
• what the Stoics meant by wanting things to be as they are
• whether acceptance is wisdom or surrender, and how you'd tell
• what becomes available once the argument with reality is over

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

• Quick intro…

events.title: Overcoming the Influences of the Past
events.summary: You already know where it came from. You’ve probably known for years. So why are you still doing it?
events.description:
You already know where it came from. You’ve probably known for years. So why are you still doing it?

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• the explanation is complete and the problem is unchanged
• they know a criticism is unfair and it still lands
• they can trace a belief to childhood and still can’t put it down
• something a friend said years ago still stings on recall
• understanding the cause turned out not to be the cure

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — concedes more than you’d expect. Children really do need attention and love, and being deprived of it really does damage them. The past was not nothing. But adversity alone didn’t produce the problem. What happened to you, multiplied by what you concluded about it, is what produced it. And the conclusion is the part still running today.

We’ll get into:
• why two people can be rejected the same way and turn out differently
• the difference between being sad about something and being hurt by it
• why concern and caring are useful, and where they tip into anxiety
• how “it is bad that I acted badly” becomes “I am bad”
• why insight into the cause so rarely fixes anything

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 7 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonable way to see the world.

events.title: Tackling Your Dire Needs for Romantic Love
events.summary: (The book titles this chapter “Is Reason Always Reasonable?” — we’ll be reading it for what it says about love.)
events.description:
(The book titles this chapter “Is Reason Always Reasonable?” — we’ll be reading it for what it says about love.)

You can be sharp, capable, and clear-headed about almost everything.
And then there’s this.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• they’re competent everywhere except here
• they test someone to see whether he’ll stay
• ordinary behavior starts looking like evidence he’s leaving
• they’re waiting, quietly, to be found out
• one person’s exit becomes a verdict on them
• they push hard enough that the thing they feared happens

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — follows one woman through this in detail. Marlow is twenty-three, runs a corporation president’s office, and is convinced she’s worthless. So when a good man loves her, she can’t believe it, tests him constantly, and drives him off. Then takes his leaving as proof she was right. Wanting love was never her problem. Needing it to decide what she was worth is what closed the loop.

We’ll get into:
• how two bad experiences turn into a rule about everyone
• the circular logic that makes being left feel like evidence
• the difference between asking someone to love you and demanding it
• why two years of analyzing her childhood never touched the jealousy
• what has to come first, being loved or accepting yourself

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 8 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonable way to see the world.

events.title: Refusing to Feel Desperately Unhappy
events.summary: There’s a word sitting in front of “unhappy,” and most of the time we don’t hear it. Desperately unhappy. Not very unhappy. Not deeply, not badly. Desperately. It’s a stronger word than we usually notice ourselves reaching for, and this…
events.description:
There’s a word sitting in front of “unhappy,” and most of the time we don’t hear it.
Desperately unhappy. Not very unhappy. Not deeply, not badly. Desperately. It’s a stronger word than we usually notice ourselves reaching for, and this chapter argues that the gap between the two makes all the difference.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• a hard week quietly becomes a judgment on their whole life
• disappointment shows up with a prediction attached about everything that follows
• sitting with the feeling makes it deeper rather than lighter
• talking themselves down feels like denying that it mattered
• everyone else’s encouragement makes it land harder, not softer

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — opens this chapter by admitting what it can’t do. Nobody can tell you how to be happy, because what you enjoy is yours alone. What it claims instead is narrower and stranger: it can tell you how to stop making yourself miserable. Sorrow at a real loss is healthy and stays. What gets added on top is a demand that the loss shouldn’t have happened, and that addition is where the despair comes from.

We’ll get into:
• the two different things we both call “unhappy”
• what the word “awful” actually claims, and why it can’t be true
• why calling a loss unfortunate moves you and calling it awful freezes you
• whether this holds up for the serious losses, not just the small ones
• why getting the thing you must have doesn’t end the anxiety

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 9 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discus…

events.title: Tackling Your Dire Need for Approval
events.summary: Nine people liked it. One didn’t. Guess which one you’re still thinking about at eleven o’clock.
events.description:
Nine people liked it. One didn’t.
Guess which one you’re still thinking about at eleven o’clock.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• one piece of criticism outweighs a dozen compliments
• a short conversation stays with them long after everyone else has forgotten it
• they wait to see how something lands before deciding what they think of it
• being liked wears off, and needs renewing
• what they say comes out gentler than what they thought
• how one person treats them becomes information about their worth

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — opens this chapter by picking a fight with the rest of psychology. Everyone says people need approval. Ellis says they want it, badly, and that the two words describe completely different situations. Children genuinely need it. Adults confused the two and never updated. Most of the chapter follows one man who spent forty years trying to secure enough of it, and what happened when the supply ran out.

We’ll get into:
• what the word “need” actually means, and why wanting isn’t that
• where psychology mixed up what children require with what adults do
• why the harder you work for approval, the less of it comes back
• what Ellis did when a client asked him to supply it
• how to take a fair criticism without it becoming a verdict

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 10 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonable way to see the world.

events.title: How to Feel Frustrated but Not Depressed or Enraged
events.summary: It was unfair. That part isn’t up for debate. The question is what happened between the unfairness and the hours you spent furious about it.
events.description:
It was unfair. That part isn’t up for debate.
The question is what happened between the unfairness and the hours you spent furious about it.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• the complaint is completely justified and changes nothing
• being right about it hasn’t made anything better
• they can be reasonable about a real injustice and lose an afternoon to a small one
• the anger arrives already convinced it’s justified
• “I can’t stand this” turns up long before any evidence for it
• they’d defend the anger as reasonable and still not want to feel it

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — takes a hard line on the thing underneath the anger. It isn’t the unfairness, which may be perfectly real. It’s the rule you’ve attached to it. It may well be unethical, Ellis says, but who decided that people absolutely must not act unjustly? You did. Drop the rule and the frustration stays. The fury doesn’t.

We’ll get into:
• the difference between “I don’t like this” and “this must not be”
• why being right about the unfairness doesn’t get you anywhere
• what Ellis told a woman whose husband genuinely did treat her badly
• how a grief can be kept alive for twenty-five years
• where acceptance stops and giving up begins

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 13 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonable way to see the world.

events.title: Controlling Your Own Emotional Destiny
events.summary: “They made me feel like an idiot.” We say things like this constantly, and almost never notice the claim buried in them. That someone else reached inside and operated the controls.
events.description:
“They made me feel like an idiot.”
We say things like this constantly, and almost never notice the claim buried in them. That someone else reached inside and operated the controls.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• the same remark from two different people lands two completely different ways
• something that would have wrecked them at twenty-five barely registers now
• they can watch someone else shrug off exactly what ruined their week
• a mood arrives on a quiet afternoon with nothing obvious behind it
• the feeling seems to come fully formed, with no gap to intervene in
• “you made me feel” is how they’d describe it, and it’s how it felt

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — spends this chapter on a client who insists his depressions arrive unannounced and unconsciously, and cannot be caught. Ellis agrees he can’t catch them in advance. Then asks him a few questions about the afternoon in question, and the sentence that started it surfaces in about a minute. Most of what we call unconscious isn’t buried, he argues. It’s just never been looked at directly.

We’ll get into:
• what actually happens between what someone does and how you feel
• why a mood can seem to come from nowhere and still have a sentence under it
• where Ellis thinks Freud went too far about the unconscious
• why you don’t feel like talking yourself out of a bad mood once you’re in one
• the honest limit, and where this claim stops being true

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 14 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not thera…

events.title: Conquering Anxiety and Panic
events.summary: Your heart is going. Your chest is tight. Something is definitely wrong. Both of those are true right up until the last three words.
events.description:
Your heart is going. Your chest is tight. Something is definitely wrong.
Both of those are true right up until the last three words.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• most of what they’re anxious about isn’t danger at all, it’s what someone might think
• the fear outlasted the thing that caused it, by years
• worrying feels like doing something, and stopping feels reckless
• knowing it has happened before and passed makes no difference while it’s happening
• they’ve become afraid of the anxiety itself
• telling themselves to relax is about as effective as telling themselves to be taller

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — spends this chapter with a woman whose fear made perfect sense for twenty years and then stopped making sense. Her father was violent. Her first husband was worse. Her second husband is gentle, her daughters are fine, and she lives in constant terror anyway. She explains it as conditioning, like Pavlov’s dogs. Ellis doesn’t accept that. If nothing out there is still feeding the fear, he asks, who is keeping it alive?

We’ll get into:
• the difference between fear that keeps you alive and anxiety that doesn’t
• whether worrying has ever prevented anything
• why the fear outlasts the danger that made sense of it
• what the word “conditioning” covers up, according to Ellis
• how you end up anxious about being anxious

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 15 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonab…

events.title: Acquiring Self-Discipline
events.summary: You know exactly what you should be doing. Not in general — the specific thing. The email, the appointment, the work you moved to tomorrow yesterday. It came to mind while you read that first line, which is the whole problem: knowing has…
events.description:
You know exactly what you should be doing.
Not in general — the specific thing. The email, the appointment, the work you moved to tomorrow yesterday. It came to mind while you read that first line, which is the whole problem: knowing has never been the missing piece.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• they’re waiting to feel like it, and have been waiting a while
• the thing they avoid takes less time than the avoiding does
• once they finally start, it’s rarely as bad as the weeks of not starting
• an outside deadline gets it done immediately, when nothing else could
• they’ve read about this, made a system for it, and abandoned the system
• putting things off has stopped feeling like something they do and started feeling like who they are

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — opens this chapter with a line worth sitting with: the easy way out is often just that, the easy way out of the most rewarding life. The argument that follows isn’t about virtue. It’s about arithmetic. A man pulls his hand back rather than risk reaching for someone’s, feels relief for about a second, and then dislikes himself for the rest of the night. The easy option was more expensive. Ellis’s name for the alternative isn’t discipline or willpower. It’s long-range hedonism: not less pleasure, more of it, counted over a longer stretch.

We’ll get into:
• why the easy way so often turns out to be the longer one
• what Ellis said to a client who wanted him to handle a breakup on his behalf
• whether any of this is moralizing, or just how the world works
• why starting is the hardest part, and what to expect from it
• the opposite error, doing things the hard way to feel noble about it

No reading requ…

events.title: Rewriting Your Personal History
events.summary: “Let’s face it, reality often stinks.” That’s the opening line. The chapter doesn’t walk it back, and it doesn’t offer to make the facts nicer than they are.
events.description:
“Let’s face it, reality often stinks.”
That’s the opening line. The chapter doesn’t walk it back, and it doesn’t offer to make the facts nicer than they are.

Why do so many thoughtful, self-aware, well-read people find that:
• they’re right about the person, and being right has never once helped
• the criticism meant to fix the situation has made it worse
• they spend more energy on someone else’s decisions than their own
• they’re waiting for things to be fair before they get on with anything
• they want the best option, so they take none of them
• the thing they’re complaining about isn’t quite the thing that’s wrong

A Guide to Rational Living — the 1961 book that became the foundation of modern cognitive therapy — spends this chapter on a woman whose mother is spending an inheritance badly. Laura is probably right about that. She wants it stopped. Ellis asks a question she hasn’t considered: does her mother have the right to be wrong? Then a harder one. If you could actually force people to stop making their own mistakes, what kind of world would you be living in, and would you want to live there?

We’ll get into:
• whether other people have a right to be wrong
• why being right about someone so rarely changes them
• what Epictetus said about this, which Ellis quotes approvingly
• the world you’d have to build to stop people making mistakes
• why the complaint on the surface is often not the real one

No reading required. We listen to the chapter together.

The plan for the night:
• Quick intro from me — who I am, and where these ideas came from
• We listen to Chapter 18 together (~20 min)
• Small-group discussion (~20 min)
• Q&A and open discussion

Not therapy. No diagnosis. Nothing you have to share. Just a good book and a more reasonable way to see the world.
